title: II. Smerdyakov With A Guitar
paragraphs: He really had no time to lose. Even as he was saying goodbye to Lise, the thought had struck him that he needed to come up with some stratagem to find his brother Dmitri, who was evidently avoiding him. It was getting late — nearly three o'clock. Alyosha's whole soul was pulled toward the monastery, toward his dying saint, but the necessity of finding Dmitri outweighed everything else. The conviction that a great, inevitable catastrophe was about to happen grew stronger in Alyosha's mind with every passing hour. What that catastrophe was, and what he would actually say to his brother when the moment came, he couldn't have said for certain. “Even if my benefactor has to die without me, at least I won't spend the rest of my life reproaching myself for the thought that I could have saved something and didn't — that I walked past and hurried home instead. If I do what I intend, I'll be following his great teaching.”

His plan was to catch his brother Dmitri off guard — to climb over the fence, just as he had the day before, slip into the garden, and settle in the summerhouse. If Dmitri weren't there, Alyosha thought, he wouldn't announce himself to Foma or the women of the house, but would stay hidden in the summerhouse, even if it meant waiting there until evening. If, as before, Dmitri were lying in wait for Grushenka to arrive, he'd very likely come to the summerhouse. Alyosha didn't dwell on the details of his plan, but resolved to act on it — even if it meant not making it back to the monastery that day.

Everything went smoothly. He climbed over the fence at almost the same spot as the day before and stole into the summerhouse unnoticed. He didn't want to be seen. The woman of the house and Foma too, if he was there, might be loyal to his brother and follow his instructions, and therefore refuse to let Alyosha into the garden, or warn Dmitri that he was being asked after.

The summerhouse was empty. Alyosha sat down and began to wait. He looked around, and somehow the place struck him as a great deal more ancient than before. Though the day was just as fine as yesterday, this time the summerhouse seemed a wretched little spot. There was a ring on the table, left no doubt by the glass of brandy that had been spilled the day before. Foolish, irrelevant thoughts drifted through his mind, the way they always do during tedious waiting. He wondered, for instance, why he had sat down in precisely the same place as before, rather than in the other seat. Finally he felt very low — weighed down by suspense and uncertainty. But he hadn't been sitting there more than a quarter of an hour when he suddenly heard the strumming of a guitar somewhere quite close. People were sitting, or had just sat down, somewhere in the bushes no more than twenty paces away. Alyosha suddenly remembered that on coming out of the summerhouse the day before, he had caught a glimpse of an old, low, green garden bench among the bushes on the left, by the fence. The people must be sitting on it now. But who were they?
A man's voice suddenly began singing in a sugary falsetto, accompanying himself on the guitar:
With invincible force I am bound to my dear. O Lord, have mercy On her and on me! On her and on me! On her and on me!
The voice stopped. It was a lackey's tenor and a lackey's song. Another voice — a woman's — suddenly asked with insinuating, bashful, but affected mincing:
“Why haven't you been to see us for so long, Pavel Fyodorovitch? Why do you always look down on us?”

“Not at all,” answered the man's voice politely, but with an emphatic dignity. It was clear that he had the upper hand and that the woman was making the advances. “I believe that must be Smerdyakov,” thought Alyosha, “from his voice. And the lady must be the daughter of the house here — the one who came from Moscow, the one who wears the dress with a tail and goes to Marfa for soup.”
“I'm awfully fond of verses of all kinds, as long as they rhyme,” the woman's voice went on. “Why don't you go on?”
The man sang again:
What do I care for royal wealth If but my dear one be in health? Lord have mercy On her and on me! On her and on me! On her and on me!
“It was even better last time,” the woman's voice observed. “You sang ‘If my darling be in health’ — that sounded more tender. I suppose you've forgotten today.”
“Poetry is rubbish!” Smerdyakov snapped.
“Oh, no! I'm very fond of poetry.”

“Insofar as it's poetry, it's essentially rubbish. Think about it — who ever talks in rhyme? And if we were all to talk in rhyme, even by government decree, we wouldn't say much, would we? Poetry is no good, Marya Kondratyevna.”
“How clever you are! How did you manage to go so deep into everything?” The woman's voice became more and more insinuating.

“I could have done better than this. I could have known more than this, if it hadn't been for my destiny from my childhood on. I'd have shot a man in a duel if he called me names for being descended from a filthy beggar and having no father. They used to throw it in my teeth back in Moscow — it had reached them from here, thanks to Grigory Vassilyevitch. Grigory Vassilyevitch blames me for rebelling against my birth, but I'd have authorized them to kill me before I was born, so I wouldn't have come into the world at all. They used to say in the market — and your mamma too, with great lack of delicacy, would start telling me — that her hair was like a mat on her head and that she was short of five foot by a wee bit. Why say ‘a wee bit,’ when she could have said ‘a little bit,’ like everyone else? She wanted to make it touching — a regular peasant's sentiment. Can a Russian peasant be said to have feelings in comparison with an educated man? He can't be said to have any feelings at all, in his ignorance. Ever since I was a child, when I hear ‘a wee bit,’ I'm ready to burst with rage. I hate all of Russia, Marya Kondratyevna.”
“If you'd been a cadet in the army, or a young hussar, you wouldn't talk like that — you'd draw your saber to defend all of Russia.”
“I don't want to be a hussar, Marya Kondratyevna, and what's more, I'd like to abolish all soldiers.”
“And when an enemy comes, who's going to defend us?”

“There's no need for defense. In 1812 there was a great invasion of Russia by Napoleon, the first Emperor of the French, the father of the present one, and it would have been a good thing if they'd conquered us. A clever nation would have conquered a very stupid one and annexed it. We'd have had quite different institutions.”

“Are they really so much better in their own country than we are? I wouldn't trade a certain dandy I know of for three young Englishmen,” Marya Kondratyevna observed tenderly, no doubt accompanying the words with a most languishing glance.
“That's as one prefers.”
“But you are just like a foreigner — like a most gentlemanly foreigner. I'm telling you that, even though it makes me bashful.”

“If you want to know, the folks there and ours here are just alike in their vice. They're all swindlers, only there the scoundrel wears polished boots and here he grovels in filth and sees no harm in it. The Russian people need a thrashing, as Fyodor Pavlovitch said quite truly yesterday, though he's mad, and all his children too.”
“You said yourself that you had such respect for Ivan Fyodorovitch.”

“But he called me a stinking lackey. He thinks I might be unruly. He's mistaken about that. If I had a certain sum in my pocket, I'd have left here long ago. Dmitri Fyodorovitch is lower than any lackey — in his behavior, in his mind, and in his poverty. He doesn't know how to do anything, and yet everyone respects him. I may be only a soup-maker, but with luck I could open a café restaurant on the Petrovka in Moscow, because my cookery is something special, and there's no one in Moscow, apart from the foreigners, whose cookery is anything special. Dmitri Fyodorovitch is a beggar, but if he were to challenge the son of the top count in the country, he'd fight him. And in what way is he actually better than I am? He's much stupider than I am. Look at the money he's wasted without any need!”
“It must be lovely, a duel,” Marya Kondratyevna observed suddenly.
“How so?”

“It must be so dreadful and so brave, especially when young officers with pistols in their hands pop at one another for some lady's sake. A perfect picture! Ah, if only girls were allowed to watch, I'd give anything to see one!”
“It's all very well when you're firing at someone, but when he's firing straight into your mug, you'd feel pretty silly. You'd be glad to run away, Marya Kondratyevna.”
“You don't mean to say you'd run away?” But Smerdyakov didn't deign to reply. After a moment's silence the guitar tinkled again, and he began to sing once more in the same falsetto:
Whatever you may say, I shall go far away. Life will be bright and gay In the city far away. I shall not grieve, I shall not grieve at all, I don't intend to grieve at all.

Then something unexpected happened. Alyosha suddenly sneezed. They fell silent. Alyosha got up and walked toward them. He found Smerdyakov dressed up and wearing polished boots, his hair pomaded, and perhaps even curled. The guitar was lying on the garden bench. His companion was the daughter of the house, wearing a light-blue dress with a train two yards long. She was young and wouldn't have been bad-looking, but for the fact that her face was so round and terribly freckled.
“Will my brother Dmitri be back soon?” Alyosha asked, with as much composure as he could manage.
Smerdyakov got up slowly; Marya Kondratyevna rose too.
“How am I supposed to know about Dmitri Fyodorovitch? It's not as though I were his keeper,” Smerdyakov answered quietly, distinctly, and with contempt.
“But I'm simply asking whether you do know,” Alyosha explained.
“I know nothing of his whereabouts and don't want to.”
“But my brother told me you keep him informed of everything that goes on in the house, and that you promised to let him know when Agrafena Alexandrovna comes.”
Smerdyakov turned a deliberate, unmoved glance on him.
“And how did you get in this time, since the gate was bolted an hour ago?” he asked, eyeing Alyosha.
“I came in from the back alley, over the fence, and went straight to the summerhouse. I hope you'll forgive me,” he added, turning to Marya Kondratyevna. “I was in a hurry to find my brother.”

“Ach, how could we ever hold it against you!” drawled Marya Kondratyevna, flattered by Alyosha's apology. “Dmitri Fyodorovitch often goes to the summerhouse that very way. We don't even know he's here, and he'll be sitting in the summerhouse.”
“I'm very anxious to find him, or to learn from you where he is now. Believe me, it's on business of great importance to him.”
“He never tells us,” lisped Marya Kondratyevna.

“Even though I come here as a friend,” Smerdyakov began again, “Dmitri Fyodorovitch has pestered me mercilessly, even here, with his constant questions about the master. ‘What's the news?’ he'll ask. ‘What's going on in there now? Who's coming and going?’ And can't I tell him a bit more? Twice already he's threatened me with death.”
“With death?” Alyosha exclaimed, startled.

“Do you think he'd think much of that, with his temper, which you had a chance to see for yourself yesterday? He says if I let Agrafena Alexandrovna in and she spends the night there, I'll be the first to pay for it. I'm terribly afraid of him, and if I weren't even more afraid of doing it, I ought to let the police know. God only knows what he might do!”
“His honor told him the other day, ‘I'll pound you in a mortar!’” Marya Kondratyevna added.
“Oh, if it's pounding in a mortar, it may be only talk,” Alyosha observed. “If I could meet him, I might speak to him about that too.”

“Well, the only thing I can tell you is this,” said Smerdyakov, as if thinking better of it. “I'm here as an old friend and neighbor, and it would be strange if I didn't come. On the other hand, Ivan Fyodorovitch sent me first thing this morning to your brother's lodgings in Lake Street, without a letter, but with a message telling Dmitri Fyodorovitch to come dine with him at the restaurant here in the market-place. I went, but I didn't find Dmitri Fyodorovitch at home, even though it was eight o'clock. ‘He was here, but he's quite gone,’ those were the very words of his landlady. It's as if there's some understanding between them. Perhaps at this very moment he's at the restaurant with Ivan Fyodorovitch, because Ivan Fyodorovitch hasn't been home to dinner, and Fyodor Pavlovitch dined alone an hour ago and has gone to lie down. But I beg you most particularly not to mention me or what I've told you, because he'd kill me for nothing at all.”
“Brother Ivan invited Dmitri to the restaurant today?” Alyosha repeated quickly.
“That's right.”
“The Metropolis tavern in the market-place?”
“The very same.”
“That's quite likely,” Alyosha cried, much excited. “Thank you, Smerdyakov — that's important. I'll go there at once.”
“Don't betray me,” Smerdyakov called after him.
“Oh, no, I'll go to the tavern as though by chance. Don't worry.”
“But wait a moment, I'll open the gate for you,” cried Marya Kondratyevna.
“No — it's a shortcut, I'll get back over the fence.”

What he had heard threw Alyosha into great agitation. He hurried to the tavern. It was impossible for him to enter the tavern in his monastic dress, but he could inquire at the entrance for his brothers and call them down. But just as he reached the place, a window was flung open, and his brother Ivan called down to him from it.
“Alyosha, can't you come up here? I'd be awfully grateful.”
“Of course I can — only I'm not quite sure whether in this dress —”
“But I'm in a private room. Come up the steps; I'll run down to meet you.”
A minute later Alyosha was sitting beside his brother. Ivan was dining alone.
